strengths: Addresses a timely, highly practical, and under-explored challenge in robot learning: personalizing frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to manipulate user-specific items among visually similar distractors using only a few reference images.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning two simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER and Personalized-VLABench) across multiple robot embodiments and a real-world benchmark on an SO-101 robot arm with diverse everyday objects.

Well-designed and insightful baseline comparisons, particularly the adaptation of VLM token-learning (Yo'LLaVA-style soft prompts) to VLAs, accompanied by detailed token embedding space alignment metrics (CKA, cosine similarity) and cross-attention map visualizations explaining why token learning falls short in closed-loop manipulation.

Clear presentation and thorough failure mode analysis, categorizing errors into single-view perception errors, cross-view inconsistencies, and downstream manipulation failures, alongside practical wall-clock latency profiling showing minimal per-step overhead.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the method primarily chains existing off-the-shelf foundation models and perception tools (Grounding DINO, DINOv2 retrieval, SAM 2 tracking, and color tinting with template-based instruction rewriting) rather than introducing a new learning methodology.

Sensitivity and lack of native multi-view consistency: per-view 2D grounding and tracking can drift or lock onto different instances across cameras, which accounts for over 50% of all failure cases in multi-view benchmarks (Personalized-VLABench and real-world).

Reliance on color/tint prompt heuristics: overlaying a colored tint on the target object and rewriting the instruction ('the red cup') assumes the underlying VLA robustly follows color grounding without being distracted by existing scene colors or degraded by visual domain shift from semi-transparent overlays.

strengths: Clear problem formulation: The paper tackles a timely, practical, and under-explored limitation of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models—instance-level personalization to manipulate user-specific belongings among same-category distractors without retraining.

Extensive and rigorous experimental evaluation: The authors evaluate across two simulation platforms (Personalized-SIMPLER and Personalized-VLABench) across multiple robot arms, as well as a physical 6-DoF SO-101 robot arm across 8 categories with both selection and pick-and-place tasks.

Thorough baseline construction and deep diagnostic analysis: The adaptation of the token-learning baseline (Yo'LLaVA style) is remarkably rigorous, including empirical validation of embedding space preservation between PaliGemma and pi-0/pi-0.5 via CKA, kNN@1, and cosine similarity, as well as temporal cross-attention rollout visualizations to explain why token conditioning drifts or decouples from the action expert.

Practical efficiency and training-free deployment: VAP introduces minimal runtime overhead (~10% per step using SAM2 tracking) and requires zero weight updates to the underlying VLA, making it immediately usable upon registering a handful of reference images.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The core method is essentially a modular composition of existing, off-the-shelf vision foundation models (Grounding DINO for category proposals, DINOv2 for feature matching, SAM2 for segmentation/tracking) combined with a simple color tint overlay and template string replacement.

Reliance on VLA color grounding and visual tinting artifacts: Rewriting 'my X' to 'the [color] X' requires that the frozen VLA already possesses strong color-referring grounding. Overlaying a semi-transparent color tint also alters the native visual appearance of the object, which could interfere with fine-grained grasp affordances or collide with native object colors.

Lack of 3D geometric cross-view consistency: In multi-view camera setups, independent 2D grounding and tracking across views leads to frequent inconsistencies (accounting for over 50% of all failure cases in multi-view simulation and real-world experiments), which is an acknowledged architectural limitation of the per-view pipeline.

Scope limited to short-horizon tabletop settings: The evaluation is restricted to clean tabletop environments with a single target instance and 2 same-category distractors, leaving more complex clutter, severe occlusions, or multi-step personalized behaviors unaddressed.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in embodied AI: standard vision-language-action (VLA) models generalize to semantic categories ('a cup') but struggle with instance-level personalization ('my cup') in the presence of visually similar distractors.

The proposed Visual Attentive Prompting (VAP) pipeline is entirely training-free and modular, enabling immediate zero-shot deployment of frozen VLAs on novel personal objects using only a handful of reference images.

Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER on Google Robot and WidowX, Personalized-VLABench on Franka) as well as physical experiments on a real-world SO-101 robot arm.

Thorough and insightful comparative analysis: the paper compares against well-crafted hard-prompting and soft-token-learning (Yo'LLaVA-style) baselines, supported by detailed representation alignment metrics (CKA, kNN@1) and attention heatmaps explaining why token-level conditioning struggles during closed-loop VLA control.
Clear writing, transparent failure mode taxonomy (Case 1–3 breakdowns), and practical runtime profiling demonstrating minimal computational overhead (~10% per step).
weaknesses: From a methodological standpoint, the algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental: the system primarily orchestrates off-the-shelf vision foundation models (Grounding DINO, DINOv2, SAM 2) combined with a visual tinting heuristic and string substitution, rather than introducing a new architectural or policy learning formulation.

Sensitivity and robustness to prompt injection heuristics (e.g., overlaying semi-transparent color tints) are not systematically ablated, which may introduce visual artifacts or interfere with policies sensitive to natural color/lighting distributions.

Grounding is executed on independent 2D views rather than leveraging 3D geometric correspondence, leading to multi-view tracking inconsistencies that account for over 50% of the failures in multi-camera setups (as acknowledged by the authors in Table 6).

Evaluation tasks are confined to relatively simple tabletop pointing and short-horizon pick-and-place routines with single personal items, leaving long-horizon multi-step personalized interactions for future exploration.

strengths: Practical and timely problem formulation: Personal object manipulation amidst visually similar same-category distractors is a critical hurdle for deploying Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models in human-centric environments.

Effective training-free paradigm: Formulating personalization as an input-side intervention (visual highlighting + instruction rewriting) allows pre-trained, frozen VLAs to act on unseen personal items without requiring per-object robot demonstrations or parameter fine-tuning.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The method is validated across two simulation suites (Personalized-SIMPLER and Personalized-VLABench) and a physical SO-101 robot arm across multiple manipulation tasks, consistently demonstrating substantial performance gains over baselines.

Rigorously analyzed baselines and ablations: The comparison against a well-crafted soft prompt (token-learning) baseline adapted from Yo'LLaVA—supported by representation alignment metrics (CKA, kNN@1) and attention heatmaps—provides valuable insights into why token learning struggles in continuous control compared to input prompting.

Transparent error and runtime analysis: The paper includes a thorough breakdown of failure modes (e.g., control bottlenecks vs. multi-view inconsistency) and demonstrates minimal runtime overhead (0.02s tracking overhead).
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is somewhat limited: The core framework is largely a pipeline integration of existing foundation models (Grounding DINO for candidate proposal, DINOv2 for feature matching, SAM2 for tracking, and standard color overlay prompting) rather than a novel learning algorithm.

Multi-view inconsistency remains an open failure mode: Because grounding and tracking operate independently per camera view, conflicting visual prompts across different cameras account for over 50% of the failures in multi-view simulation and real-world experiments. While Appendix D details possible MAP/geometric formulations, the implemented system lacks cross-view association.

Brittleness of rule-based instruction rewriting: The language adapter assumes a relatively rigid syntactic template ('my X' -> 'the [color] X') and explicit category extraction. Its robustness to complex, open-vocabulary linguistic formulations or indirect references without explicit category nouns is not fully established.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical limitation of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models: resolving instance-level personal object manipulation among visually similar same-category distractors without retraining.
Completely training-free, inference-time approach that leaves the downstream VLA policy frozen while adding minimal latency (~0.02s per step for SAM2 tracking).

Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER on Google Robot and WidowX, Personalized-VLABench on Franka) and real-world hardware (SO-101 arm across selection and pick-and-place tasks).

Thorough and insightful baseline comparison, particularly the detailed analysis of the token-learning (Soft Prompt) baseline including token embedding alignment (CKA, cosine similarity) and spatial cross-attention heatmap visualizations.

Extensive ablations isolating key design components, including prompt geometry (mask vs. bounding box), highlight opacity, reference aggregation strategies, and the necessity of coupled vision-language alignment (mask + instruction rewriting).
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is somewhat modest: the approach essentially constructs a modular perception wrapper combining off-the-shelf vision models (Grounding DINO, DINOv2, SAM2) to identify the target, overlays a colored tint, and rewrites the command to a color-referring expression ('the red X'), thereby reducing the problem to standard color-conditioned manipulation.

Independent per-view processing leads to significant multi-view inconsistency: as shown in Table 6 and Table 9, 50–59% of failures in multi-view setups stem from contradictory prompt masks across camera viewpoints, for which the current method provides no explicit fusion or 3D consistency mechanism.

Instruction rewriting logic relies primarily on deterministic string matching (e.g., 'my X' to 'the [color] X'); while straightforward, this template-based assumption limits robustness to open-ended or indirect linguistic personal references.

Applying an artificial color overlay in pixel space introduces a delicate trade-off between saliency and visual distortion/occlusion of fine surface textures and geometric boundaries, as reflected in the sensitivity to overlay opacity in Table 13.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in embodied robotics: enabling frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to personalize to user-specific objects among visually similar distractors without requiring expensive per-object retraining or fine-tuning.

Proposes a clean, training-free inference-time intervention (VAP) that leverages non-parametric visual reference memory, discriminative visual feature matching (DINOv2), open-vocabulary detection (Grounding DINO), and tracking (SAM2) to visually prompt the target object via mask highlighting and instruction rewriting.

Extensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across multiple robotic simulation platforms (Google Robot, WidowX, Franka arm) and real-world physical robot experiments (SO-101 arm), showing substantial gains in both Success Rate (SR) and Correct Movement Ratio (CMR) over non-personalized and language-prompting baselines.

Thorough comparison with a well-constructed soft-prompt token-learning baseline (adapted from Yo'LLaVA with PaliGemma transfer), supported by insightful analyses of embedding alignment, cross-attention heatmaps, and failure modes.

Detailed ablation studies validating key design components, including instruction rewriting, voting vs. averaging aggregation, number of reference views, mask geometry vs. bounding boxes, and highlight opacity.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is somewhat modular and engineering-driven, combining established foundation vision models (Grounding DINO, DINOv2, SAM2) with visual tint overlays and rule-based template rewrites rather than introducing new learning or policy architecture formulations.

Reliance on rule-based instruction rewriting and synthetic visual tinting ('the red X') may encounter issues if the scene or object itself heavily features that color, or if more complex, ambiguous language inputs beyond standard possessive templates ('my X') are used.

Multi-view inconsistency remains a prominent limitation: because grounding and tracking are executed independently per camera view, conflicting prompts across views account for more than 50% of failures in multi-camera simulation and real-world setups, with the proposed cross-view association left as future work.
Evaluation is currently restricted to relatively short-horizon tabletop manipulation and selection tasks with a small number of candidate distractors.
